messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leila was a 21-year-old Middle Eastern forester who had been working seasonal trail and woodland surveys when she witnessed a serious crash on a narrow service road near the edge of the state forest. She had been hiking back toward her truck at dusk when a car coming too fast rounded the bend, clipped the gravel shoulder, and struck the guardrail hard enough to leave the front end crumpled and steaming. She did not see every detail of the impact clearly, but she saw enough to know that people were hurt, and the sight of blood on the roadside and on the vehicle door stayed with her in a way she could not shake. In the first weeks afterward, even talk about accidents could jolt her; if coworkers mentioned a deer strike, a rollover, or a wreck on the county road, she felt her body tense and her attention snap outward, and she began staying up until very late so she would not have to lie in bed with the images waiting for her. The more she tried to keep herself busy and postpone sleep, the more she found herself scanning every parking lot, shoulder, and stretch of road for signs of danger, as if watching closely enough might keep something awful from happening again.

Certain reminders pulled her back with unnerving force. If she smelled hot metal, dust, or the sharp roadside odor she associated with that evening, the scene seemed to rush forward in fragments, though never as a full, orderly story. She would catch herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, and she described the recollection as belonging to someone else rather than to her, as if she were standing beside a stranger’s disaster instead of her own experience. Even so, when the memory surfaced, she felt the same unease in her stomach and an urgent need to get away from it. Those moments quickly fed her sense that she had acted in ways that went against who she was. Leila had always seen herself as careful, useful, and someone who would step in when others needed help, and she could not let go of the belief that she should have protected the people involved and failed them. That conviction darkened her mood further; she came to believe she used to be a happy person but now was always miserable, and the thought of herself as someone who had let others down sat heavily with her long after the scene had passed.

The harder she tried to avoid being overwhelmed, the more limited her life became. She began refusing invitations if she thought anyone might bring up the crash, and if coworkers started discussing roadway accidents or a recent fender-bender near the trailhead, she would find an excuse to walk away. She also stayed alert in a way that never really let up, checking her surroundings constantly even in the forest office or while loading equipment, her eyes moving to every entrance and passing vehicle. Yet the very act of trying to manage things this way seemed to keep the memory active. When she was alone at night, the unfinished fragments would return more easily; when she had stayed up too late and was exhausted, the smell, the blood, and the image of the crumpled car intruded with more vividness, and she would again feel that it was not fully her own memory. In those moments, the same belief about failing to protect others would flare back up, and with it the conviction that she had become a different, worse version of herself. The cycle made her feel trapped between guarding against danger and being haunted by what she had seen.

By the time she sought help, Leila was exhausted from the constant vigilance and from how much of her life had narrowed around avoiding reminders. She was increasingly worried that if she kept sleeping so late and keeping herself on alert, she would lose the ability to rest at all, and she feared that the crash would continue to define her every time she smelled something familiar, heard people talking about accidents, or saw damaged cars on the road. What brought her in was the sense that she was no longer just remembering what happened; she was organizing her days around keeping it away, only to find it returning with the same accusation each time. More than anything, she hoped to feel like herself again, but she was most afraid that she had permanently failed the people she saw that evening and would never stop feeling miserable because of it.
